segments.title: Where the diesel Kriegsmarine counterfactual stops
segments.body: The scenario combines two changes: an all-diesel German navy and capital ships built around the Scharnhorst hull. Its main development period is the 1930s, with the Type 1934 destroyers providing an early point of departure. Five years of different construction decisions would produce a different fleet by 1939. Once that fleet changes other countries' decisions, a fixed account of subsequent events becomes difficult to defend. Wargaming can explore those responses and supports exercises in university war studies and military planning.

evidence.note: Two combined scenarios, the Type 1934 destroyers as an early departure point, five years of different construction decisions, and the boundary between projection and wargaming.

segments.summary: Combining diesel propulsion with a common Scharnhorst capital-ship hull changes the fleet available in 1939 and limits how far events can be predicted.

segments.title: Deutschland and Scharnhorst: speed, power and endurance
segments.body: The Deutschland-class figures given here are 26 knots maximum speed and 10,000 nautical miles at 20 knots. Eight diesel engines supply a quoted 53,000 shaft horsepower. Scharnhorst is compared at 31 knots, with twelve boilers and three steam turbines. Two range figures are offered for the latter comparison, 7,100 and 6,200 nautical miles at 19 knots. These figures introduce the distinction between maximum speed and the speed a ship can sustain over a long deployment.

evidence.note: Deutschland and Scharnhorst speed, range and machinery figures, including the alternative Scharnhorst range estimates.

segments.summary: Compare the Deutschland class's diesel endurance with the higher top speed and shorter quoted range of Scharnhorst.

segments.title: Concentrating German engine development on diesels
segments.body: German marine diesel development was moving from nine-cylinder engines toward twelve- and twenty-four-cylinder machinery. An all-diesel policy would redirect work from 600 PSI boilers into those engines instead of maintaining parallel propulsion programmes. Multiple engines and gearing would provide the proposed route to the required power and speed while retaining endurance. Earlier availability of that performance depends on the counterfactual concentration of development effort. The procurement criticism is that matching other navies' machinery encouraged Germany to imitate their priorities instead of concentrating on its own strengths.

evidence.note: Larger diesel engines, geared multi-engine installations and a proposed shift away from 600 PSI boiler research, followed by criticism of German emulation of other navies.

segments.summary: The proposed shift redirects effort from advanced steam machinery into larger marine diesels and gearing.

segments.title: Diesel fuel and competition between the German services
segments.body: A naval diesel policy would reduce competition with the army and Luftwaffe, which preferred petrol and aviation fuel. The proposed political benefit is greater freedom to direct a naval fuel supply. Refining heavier ship fuel into diesel is another proposed advantage. Cracking hydrocarbons is presented as easier than reforming or hydrotreating them, although the spoken explanation uses loose refining terminology. These advantages concern the supply and allocation of naval fuel; fuel availability remains a constraint.

evidence.note: Army and Luftwaffe fuel preferences and the proposed conversion of heavier fuel into diesel. The spoken refining terminology is loose.

segments.summary: Naval diesel use is proposed as a way to reduce fuel competition with the army and Luftwaffe.

segments.title: A common fuel pool would still face diesel shortages
segments.body: A production target of 1.34 million tons a year is followed by a quoted average of 1.5 million tons during 1940-44. Average consumption is described as exceeding production by roughly 26,000 tons a year. Stores and supplies obtained elsewhere are offered as ways that gap was met. These figures do not establish a plentiful surplus for a larger fleet. The proposed advantage is that a navy using one fuel could allocate it between operations without waiting for a particular mix of diesel and heavy fuel oil. Concentrating on diesel from the mid-1930s is also expected to create a clearer case for expanding production.

evidence.note: Production target, wartime average, 26,000-ton annual consumption gap and allocation of a common naval fuel supply. The isolated 295,000-ton figure at 8:12-8:17 lacks a clear category and is not treated as comparable total production.

segments.summary: The quoted fuel balance leaves little spare diesel, but a common supply would let the navy choose which ships to operate.

segments.title: H-class battleships and Z51 as diesel precedents
segments.body: Some H-class battleship designs and the engines developed for Z51 show that large German marine diesels were part of historical design work. MAN's development includes the twenty-four-cylinder machinery discussed here. The counterfactual brings that effort forward and gives it a larger share of resources. Those projects provide a historical starting point, without establishing that the same machinery was ready throughout the early 1930s. Z51 is judged too late to affect the war as it actually unfolded.

evidence.note: Historical H-class diesel designs, MAN engine development and Z51, alongside the proposal to concentrate resources on diesel machinery earlier.

segments.summary: Historical H-class and Z51 machinery work supplies the starting point for an earlier diesel fleet.

segments.title: Diesel destroyers for the opening campaigns
segments.body: The scenario imagines diesel propulsion reaching both the Type 1934 and Type 1936 destroyer groups. Greater endurance would give those ships more options during the opening of the war and the Norwegian operations of 1940. Diesel torpedo boats extend the same proposal to smaller surface forces. The precise destroyer range quoted here is unclear, so the argument establishes an intended endurance benefit rather than a specific performance figure.

evidence.note: Hypothetical diesel Type 1934 and Type 1936 destroyers for early-war and Norwegian operations, with the same propulsion proposed for torpedo boats. The range wording at 12:27 is ambiguous.

segments.summary: Earlier diesel machinery would widen the uses of German destroyers in 1939 and during the Norwegian campaign.

segments.title: Surface ships and submarines competing for propulsion research
segments.body: German submarine development already required substantial effort on diesel-electric propulsion. Maintaining surface-ship diesels and steam machinery alongside it divided research and development among different demands. In this interpretation, pursuing a faster ship on paper diverted resources from engines Germany could already develop well. Better diesels are expected to make later Deutschland-type ships faster while preserving, or possibly increasing, their range. That expected improvement remains conditional on successful development.

evidence.note: Competing surface-diesel, submarine-diesel and steam research demands, with larger diesels expected to improve Deutschland performance without sacrificing endurance.

segments.summary: Separate surface-diesel, submarine-diesel and steam programmes frame a proposed change in research priorities.

segments.title: Why one extra knot matters on a long cruise
segments.body: The comparison returns to 10,000 nautical miles for the Deutschland class against the longer quoted Scharnhorst figure of 7,100. That is a 2,900-nautical-mile difference in total range. The diesel ship also has a quoted cruising speed of 20 knots against 19. An extra knot adds 24 nautical miles in a day and 240 over ten days. The argument treats the Deutschland machinery as an early generation with further development available, rather than the final limit of diesel performance.

evidence.note: Quoted ranges and cruising speeds, the 2,900-nautical-mile range difference, and the additional distance from one knot over a day and ten days.

segments.summary: Small cruising-speed differences accumulate over days, while additional fuel endurance enlarges the area a raider can reach.

segments.title: Tirpitz and Holtzendorff as competing strategic models
segments.body: In this interpretation, Tirpitz pursued a Royal Navy in miniature, an ambition that appealed to the Kaiser. Henning von Holtzendorff led a competing school concerned with what Germany needed and how it could achieve it. His support for unrestricted submarine warfare followed from the options available when he took charge. His school is credited with developing influential officers, including Raeder and Dönitz. The claim that almost every major German naval success in the First World War derived from his methods or pupils is an assessment of strategic influence. A deliberately polemical explanation for Tirpitz's greater prominence is that his public failures are more comfortable for British pride than Holtzendorff's effectiveness. Admiration for that effectiveness coexists with criticism of the brutality of Holtzendorff's decisions.

evidence.note: Tirpitz's prestige fleet and Holtzendorff's competing strategic school, Raeder and Dönitz as inheritors, and evaluative claims about wartime success and British historical memory.

segments.summary: A critical comparison of German admirals introduces the conflict between fleet prestige and using Germany's available strengths.

segments.title: Plan Z and the political choice behind a diesel fleet
segments.body: Plan Z embodied competing ambitions in this interpretation. One was a prestigious miniature counterpart to the Royal Navy; the other was a force suited to German requirements. Hitler's attraction to impressive new weapons complicated the political choices facing naval leaders. The counterfactual asks what happens if Raeder and Dönitz commit more fully to the efficient approach associated here with Holtzendorff. Diesel propulsion therefore depends on different strategic and political priorities as well as engineering choices.

evidence.note: Plan Z's competing priorities, Hitler's preference for prestige and novelty, and a hypothetical Raeder-Dönitz commitment to Holtzendorff's approach.

segments.summary: The scenario requires Raeder and Dönitz to favour operational efficiency more consistently when balancing capability against prestige.

segments.title: Holtzendorff's case for diesel capital ships
segments.body: Holtzendorff was a senior advocate of diesel engines for battleships and battlecruisers before the First World War. His supply argument favoured diesel as Germany's route away from coal because it would be easier to obtain in quantity than the alternative oil fuel discussed here. Germany's connection with Rudolf Diesel and its early engine development supplied another potential advantage. Strong approval of Holtzendorff's strategic judgment does not extend to every decision he made. His advocacy supplies a precedent for the later counterfactual, although he died in 1919.

evidence.note: Holtzendorff's senior advocacy of diesel capital ships before the First World War, German fuel access and early engine development, and his death in 1919.

segments.summary: Prewar advocacy of diesel battleships and battlecruisers is linked to German fuel access and engine development.

segments.title: A separate fuel priority as political bargaining power
segments.body: A navy concentrating on diesel would pursue a fuel priority that competed less directly with the other services. Greater control over supply and fewer disputes would give naval leaders more room to bargain. They could support the weaker side in an army-Luftwaffe dispute and gain influence from that support. Göring's political position and the army's institutional strength would still constrain such manoeuvring. These proposed advantages would reduce rivalry over fuel without eliminating interservice conflict.

evidence.note: Reduced fuel competition as a basis for hypothetical naval bargaining power, qualified by Göring's influence and the army's institutional strength.

segments.summary: Reduced fuel rivalry is proposed as a way for the navy to gain room to bargain between the army and Luftwaffe.

segments.title: Expanding diesel production from German fuel resources
segments.body: The supply argument favours diesel because Germany could expand its production using available resources and technology. Those resources included coal, from which versions of diesel could be produced. Concentrating naval demand on this fuel could simplify supply. Additional output would depend on that concentration, especially reduced effort on heavy ship oil. The proposal gives no quantified expansion programme or guaranteed surplus.

evidence.note: Diesel production from available fuels, including coal, and the conditional prospect of greater output if heavy ship-oil demands were reduced.

segments.summary: The supply case includes producing diesel from coal and concentrating fuel production on the navy's chosen requirement.

segments.title: Turbine manufacture, crew demands and machinery redundancy
segments.body: Steam turbines require carefully balanced blades and precise manufacture. High-pressure steam also complicates operation and crew training. Those demands support the proposed concentration on diesel warship machinery. Steam plants retain an advantage when machinery fails: other boilers can continue supplying a turbine, while boilers serving a disabled turbine can supply surviving turbines. Diesel engines are large, heavy pieces of machinery and do not duplicate that cross-supply arrangement. Multiple engines nevertheless provide their own form of redundancy.

evidence.note: Turbine manufacturing precision, steam-related operating and training demands, boiler-turbine cross-supply, and redundancy through multiple diesel engines.

segments.summary: Compare the manufacturing and operating demands of steam machinery with the different redundancy offered by multiple diesels.

segments.title: Selecting how many diesel engines drive each shaft
segments.body: The example starts with six diesel engines for a destroyer and a quoted design speed of 36 knots. Its endurance is described as roughly 5,500 nautical miles, with the cruising speed corrected verbally from 20 to 19 knots. The argument then considers twelve engines on a capital ship, four for each shaft, with larger machinery appropriate to the hull. Gearing would allow engines to be disconnected so a shaft could run on one, two, three or four engines. These figures describe proposed machinery arrangements and scaling, rather than a tested Scharnhorst conversion.

evidence.note: Six-engine destroyer design figures, a verbal correction to 19-knot cruising speed, and selectable engines per shaft in a proposed twelve-engine capital-ship installation.

segments.summary: A geared installation lets a ship disconnect engines and choose how many provide power to each shaft.

segments.title: Long-range raiders and Atlantic replenishment
segments.body: The proposed diesel fleet makes every successful breakout difficult to contain because even smaller ships could travel far from home. A 10,000-nautical-mile endurance is used to illustrate access across the Atlantic. That is voyage range, with replenishment still needed to extend operations. Altmark's support for Graf Spee supplies the example of an oiler helping a raider remain at sea. The strategic claim is that such endurance would force Britain to search and protect trade over a much larger area. Reduced friction over fuel and construction priorities is also expected to give German naval leaders more political freedom.

evidence.note: Long-range diesel ships and the wider British search problem, the Falklands distance comparison, 10,000-nautical-mile endurance, and Altmark's replenishment of Graf Spee.

segments.summary: A fleet of long-range ships would widen the Royal Navy's search problem, especially if raiders could replenish overseas.

segments.title: More usable capital ships or the largest battleship?
segments.body: An efficiency-minded German leadership could retain the large, fast Scharnhorst-type hull. The choice would be between enlarging individual ships and building six or seven viable capital ships. Germany's small historical fleet is attributed partly to its design choices in this interpretation. More hulls would create a different operational problem for Britain even if each ship were less powerful than the largest battleships. Construction throughput would therefore matter alongside the specifications of each ship.

evidence.note: A reusable Scharnhorst-type hull, six or seven viable capital ships as an alternative to the largest battleship, and hull-production volume.

segments.summary: The common-hull proposal asks whether several fast capital ships would serve Germany better than a smaller number of larger designs.

segments.title: Standard hulls and Germany's lost shipbuilding skills
segments.body: The fleet plan centres on one large Scharnhorst-type hull for carriers and capital ships, alongside destroyer and cruiser hulls. Submarine construction would concentrate on a large type adaptable to long-range and minelaying work, plus a coastal type. Standardisation would concentrate the expertise available after Versailles reduced German shipbuilding capacity. The losses affected shipyards and human skills: interrupted training, migration for work and retirement without passing on experience. Repeated designs would give the remaining engineers and naval architects a smaller set of problems to solve and improve.

evidence.note: A limited hull family, with repeated construction intended to concentrate expertise after post-Versailles losses of yards, trained personnel and institutional memory.

segments.summary: A small family of hulls is proposed as a way to concentrate scarce German design and construction expertise.

segments.title: Scharnhorst hull cycles and slipway investment
segments.body: Scharnhorst hull construction on the slipway is given as sixteen to twenty months, with eighteen months used as an approximate cycle. The counterfactual suggests that a programme beginning around 1935-36 could pass through three cycles by 1940. It also avoids some of the reinforcement and preparation required for Bismarck and the larger H-class proposals. Resources would instead go into repeating a hull that the yards already knew how to build. These are estimates for hull production, and they do not establish that every launched ship would be fitted out and ready for service.

evidence.note: Sixteen to twenty months on the slipway, an estimated three construction cycles, and resources saved by avoiding larger Bismarck and H-class slipway preparations.

segments.summary: The construction estimate uses repeated Scharnhorst hulls and avoids preparing slipways for successively larger battleships.

segments.title: Nine 11-inch guns or six 15-inch guns on the common hull
segments.body: The original ships in the proposed series would probably retain nine 11-inch guns. Their development is linked to the earlier Deutschland armament. Later ships are envisaged with six 15-inch guns in twin turrets occupying the corresponding positions. The argument assumes that designing for that arrangement would make rearming the early ships easier. It is a proposed route to standardisation, rather than a detailed demonstration that turret replacement alone would complete the conversion.

evidence.note: Proposed initial armament of nine 11-inch guns and later six 15-inch guns, with assumed turret compatibility simplifying upgrades.

segments.summary: The armament proposal retains the initial 11-inch installation while allowing later ships to use twin 15-inch turrets.

segments.title: The estimate of ten to twelve hulls by 1940
segments.body: The production argument suggests as many as ten hulls by 1940, with twelve offered as a further possibility. It assumes an expansion from the original two suitable slipways to four and eventually perhaps six. The estimate does not assume that every hull would be completed and operational by 1940. Ten hulls could include three carriers, while the twelve-hull version allows roughly four or five. The illustrative mixes vary as the argument develops, so they should not be read as one fixed fleet list. Diesel-powered destroyers would give the resulting carrier and capital-ship groups escorts for long Atlantic operations.

evidence.note: Ten- and twelve-hull estimates based on expanding slipway capacity, with alternative carrier shares and a distinction between hull production and operational completion.

segments.summary: The projected build programme produces alternative mixes of carriers and fast capital ships, with completion dates left uncertain.

segments.title: Turning endurance into a usable combat radius
segments.body: Long-range German forces would require Britain to patrol the approaches to the Atlantic more closely. Once through, they would have many possible operating areas. The rule of thumb here allocates roughly one third of endurance to reaching the target area, one third to returning and one third to combat operations. On that basis, the cited 3,900-nautical-mile range difference implies about 1,300 nautical miles of operating radius. Replenishment by an Altmark-type support ship would change the calculation further. The figures are an illustration of planning constraints, not a precise fuel budget for a particular sortie.

evidence.note: Atlantic approaches, a rule allocating range in thirds, the cited 3,900-mile reduction and Altmark-type replenishment. The radius figure at 41:09 is incomplete in the captions.

segments.summary: A simple division of fuel between outward passage, operations and return explains why extra range matters after an Atlantic breakout.

segments.title: Sizing capital ships for raiding and likely opponents
segments.body: The common-hull capital ship would have a maximum of six 15-inch guns in this proposal. Its usefulness depends on what Germany intends it to do. Commerce raiding and possible fighting against French or Russian forces provide different requirements from defeating the Royal Navy in a fleet action. The argument favours enough ships to carry out those missions over making each one the most powerful possible battleship. It questions whether the funding and development devoted to a larger individual design would produce better results than more Scharnhorst-type hulls.

evidence.note: Six 15-inch guns assessed against trade attack and possible French or Russian opponents, with individual ship power weighed against the number of Scharnhorst hulls.

segments.summary: Six 15-inch guns are assessed against trade warfare and possible French or Russian opponents, rather than an assumed decisive battle with Britain.

segments.title: Carrier-supported raiding groups
segments.body: The proposed fleet could send out several groups built around a carrier and two fast capital ships. Aircraft would provide reconnaissance, air defence and long-range attack, while the capital ships protected the group against surface pursuit. British battlecruisers are treated as the main ships fast enough to catch it, though fighting two German capital ships would be dangerous. Renown's historical success is qualified by the orders constraining her opponents. Aircraft would help the raiders find convoys without an R-class battleship escort or attack that escort from a distance. These capabilities belong to the counterfactual force.

evidence.note: A carrier and two fast capital ships, their reconnaissance and attack roles, the orders qualifying Renown's historical success, and choices when approaching battleship-escorted convoys.

segments.summary: A carrier and two fast capital ships would combine reconnaissance, air attack and surface protection to choose which convoys to engage.

segments.title: Bismarck's complexity and the case for more hulls
segments.body: Bismarck is recognised as a capable 15-inch-gun battleship, while her size and complexity are criticised. Her many requirements are attributed to a design process in which numerous participants wanted their preferences included. Standardising a less elaborate capital ship is proposed as a way to obtain more hulls. Even with six 15-inch guns or nine 11-inch guns, each is judged a threat that Britain would need a fast battleship to defeat reliably. Seven or eight such ships with several carriers would create a much larger interception problem. This is an assessment of the proposed force, rather than a calculated production forecast or a guarantee of combat outcomes.

evidence.note: Criticism of Bismarck's design process, the proposed gain in numbers through standardisation, and the judgment that British fast battleships would be needed against the resulting capital ships.

segments.summary: Simpler capital-ship requirements are proposed as a way to create more threats for Britain's fast battleships to cover.

segments.title: Graf Zeppelin's air group and integration risks
segments.body: A Graf Zeppelin-style air group is considered feasible on the Scharnhorst-based carrier. The objection concerns the systems used to carry and support it. Many unfamiliar ideas would have to work together on their first installation, making integration an operational risk. French carrier design provides an example of ingenious arrangements judged inconvenient in service. The criticism is that the proposed system leaves too little tolerance for the technology and people of the period. Successful integration remains possible, but fitting the aircraft aboard would not by itself establish a useful carrier.

evidence.note: Air-group capacity distinguished from the integration of aircraft support systems, with French carrier practice supplying a critical comparison.

segments.summary: A Scharnhorst-sized carrier could carry the proposed air group, but its aircraft-handling systems would still have to work together.

segments.title: Diesel destroyer endurance and the Narvik problem
segments.body: The proposed raiding forces become more useful if destroyers can accompany them on outward and return passages. A suitable cruiser could escort the carrier throughout a longer operation. The endurance comparison moves from roughly 2,000 nautical miles to more than 5,000, though the accompanying cruising-speed figure is unclear. Narvik supplies the warning: lack of fuel is identified as the reason the German destroyers remained exposed there. Some diesel destroyer projects are dated to 1938-39 or earlier, with their introduction delayed by a complicated approval process and repeated concern about matching steam-turbine top speeds. The practical preference is a 34-knot destroyer that can join an operation over a 36-knot ship without the range to participate.

evidence.note: Escort endurance, fuel shortages at Narvik, diesel projects dated to 1938-39 or earlier, and the preference for usable range over a 36-knot maximum. The 90-knot caption at 47:32 leaves the diesel cruising-speed figure unclear.

segments.summary: Greater destroyer endurance would support Atlantic raiding groups and address the fuel constraint illustrated by Narvik.

segments.title: Matching warship procurement to national needs
segments.body: An impressive foreign capability is wasted money if it does not meet a navy's requirements. The German destroyer example connects that procurement judgment to the range needed for a mission. Adapting an existing design offers a way to obtain suitable capabilities without designing an entirely new ship. Canadian and Australian versions of Type 26 supply examples. Type 31, Mogami variations and FREMM variants extend the comparison.

evidence.note: National requirements and adaptation of common designs, with Canadian and Australian Type 26 variants, Type 31, Mogami and FREMM as examples.

segments.summary: The destroyer debate leads to a wider procurement question: does an attractive capability meet the purchasing navy's requirements?

segments.title: A raiding fleet needs escorts with matching reach
segments.body: German destroyer thinking is criticised for remaining tied to short-range torpedo-boat operations in the Baltic and coastal waters. That outlook fits poorly with the long-distance raiding role associated with the Deutschland class and other surface ships. Diesel propulsion is offered as a way to give escorts the range their task requires. Even raiders operating independently would need screening during part of their passage. Destroyers could add anti-aircraft and anti-surface fire support while the larger ships crossed confined approaches.

evidence.note: Coastal destroyer assumptions conflict with surface-raider needs for screening and additional anti-aircraft and anti-surface fire during transit.

segments.summary: Destroyers designed around coastal operations would restrict a fleet intended to send surface raiders into the Atlantic.

segments.title: A hypothetical German seizure of Iceland
segments.body: Greater destroyer range raises the possibility of a simultaneous German move against Denmark, Norway and Iceland. Possession of Iceland would complicate Arctic convoys and could make retaking it an early major Allied amphibious operation. The beaches are described as difficult places for landing craft. The proposed initial occupation need not involve a large formation because Iceland lacked its own army. Removing an established garrison would be another matter. This is a consequence explored within the alternate fleet scenario, with no claim that Germany historically carried out such an invasion.

evidence.note: Hypothetical simultaneous moves against Iceland, Denmark and Norway, with consequences for Arctic convoys, landing conditions and recapture.

segments.summary: The greater operating radius raises an Iceland scenario that would change Allied convoy protection and amphibious priorities.

segments.title: British construction priorities under a stronger German threat
segments.body: The German force envisaged here would change British construction priorities. Churchill would face much stronger objections to applying a First World War precedent for pausing major warships. The first three King George V-class battleships and the Illustrious-class carriers are treated as programmes that would have to continue. Some later ships might still be delayed. The argument therefore requires a British response to the new threat instead of carrying the historical construction sequence unchanged into the scenario.

evidence.note: Proposed German strength and continued early King George V and Illustrious construction. The date at 53:19 and later-ship list at 53:52-53:54 are unclear in the captions.

segments.summary: Seven German fast capital ships and three carriers would make pauses in British battleship and carrier construction harder to justify.

segments.title: French and Italian reactions to German carriers
segments.body: France would have reason to watch Germany's carrier construction closely. The scenario suggests Joffre might avoid postponement if the alternative were letting Germany acquire a modern operational carrier first. Mussolini is described as having held the ministerial authority needed to promote an Italian carrier, while showing little desire to do so. Rivalry with Hitler could alter that preference. Their competition is illustrated by the account of Mussolini declaring war on the United States before Hitler. These examples develop possible reactions to the fleet programme rather than establish a fixed sequence of new carrier orders.

evidence.note: Possible avoidance of Joffre's postponement and a prestige-driven Italian carrier response, grounded in Mussolini's ministerial authority and rivalry with Hitler.

segments.summary: A German carrier programme could influence French procurement and Mussolini's priorities through strategic concern and prestige.

segments.title: Why the Norwegian campaign would also change
segments.body: A German fleet with carriers and more Scharnhorst-type ships would make the invasion of Norway a different operation. British forces would also have reasons to act differently. Earlier moves to secure Norwegian ports or lay mines in coastal waters become possibilities. The changed ships cannot be inserted into the historical campaign while assuming every opposing decision remains the same.

evidence.note: Additional German carriers and fast capital ships could prompt earlier British seizure of Norwegian ports or coastal minelaying.

segments.summary: Additional German carriers and fast capital ships would change British choices before and during operations in Norway.

segments.title: Building the diesel-fleet wargame
segments.body: Once too many decisions change, the fleet becomes a wargaming problem. Figures from Z51 and other diesel projects provide starting assumptions for a Scharnhorst-sized capital ship and carrier. The same process can then be applied to smaller vessels in the fleet. In Alex Clarke's account of games played with friends, even one task group breaking into the North Atlantic disrupted operations until the British side located and dealt with it. That experience illustrates the modelled problem; it does not validate every performance assumption or predict a historical outcome.

evidence.note: German diesel-project figures supply fleet assumptions. Games played with friends produced severe disruption after a successful Atlantic breakout.

segments.summary: German diesel projects provide assumptions for a wargame that tests how a long-range task group would affect the North Atlantic.

segments.title: Force H and British resource strain in the wargame
segments.body: Finding enough ships to form Force H after France falls becomes difficult in the described wargame. Britain is still judged to possess enough resources to prevail, provided major-ship construction continues. The stronger threat encourages retention of every useful ship and can lead to completion of Lion-class battleships. French forces also tend to operate farther outside the Mediterranean before Italy enters the war. That changes where those ships are when France falls and raises further questions about their fate. Repeated versions produced serious British allocation problems without establishing a German victory.

evidence.note: Simulated Force H allocation pressure, British resource advantages, possible Lion completion, altered French deployments and repeated scenario trials.

segments.summary: The simulated raiding threat competes with other British deployments and changes the construction and disposition of Allied fleets.

segments.title: Churchill and plans that assume perfect execution
segments.body: The criticism of Churchill here concerns clever schemes that depend on everything going to plan. It credits his intelligence while questioning whether the people carrying out a plan could meet its ideal assumptions. Ordinary human limitations would remain even when a proposal worked brilliantly in its designer's head. The warning appears during the diesel-fleet wargame, where Britain would need all its available resources to meet the enlarged German threat.

evidence.note: An assessment of Churchill's intelligence and plans dependent on ideal execution, followed by the resource demands of the diesel-fleet scenario.

segments.summary: A criticism of Churchill's planning connects attractive ideas with the limits of the people expected to carry them out.

segments.title: A simulated Atlantic raid supported by disguised oilers
segments.body: Alex Clarke recalls commanding a raiding force whose Scharnhorst-based capital ships and carriers had an assumed range of roughly 12,000 nautical miles at 21 knots. The figure is an approximate recollection of the game settings. The force included three cruisers, four destroyers and oilers disguised as merchant ships. Those supply vessels entered ports under false national identities, obtained supplies and returned to replenish the force. It took the British player about thirty turns to confine the raiders, after roughly two dozen convoys had been destroyed across the North and South Atlantic. These are simulated events and losses, not historical performance or a forecast.

evidence.note: Remembered game assumptions, escorts and disguised oilers, followed by about thirty turns and roughly two dozen destroyed convoys in one simulated raid. The captioned cruiser designation is unclear.

segments.summary: One wargame run illustrates the reach of a diesel raiding force and the replenishment system that kept it moving.

segments.title: A hypothetical Lion with diesel and turbine machinery
segments.body: Other navies would reconsider their own requirements after recognising the endurance of the proposed German fleet. One version of the wargame therefore tested a different machinery arrangement for a Lion-class battleship. Diesel engines would provide cruising power through gearing, with turbines used for high speed. This experimental arrangement was tested within the alternate scenario. It illustrates how a German propulsion decision could change British ship design as well as operations.

evidence.note: Hypothetical Lion propulsion tested in the wargame, with geared diesels for cruising and turbines for high speed.

segments.summary: One tested British response uses diesels for cruising and turbines for high speed in a hypothetical Lion-class battleship.
